title: Execution contexts, call stack, and hoisting
hook: Every function call pushes a frame onto the call stack inside an execution context. Variable environment, scope chain, and hoisting rules determine what names resolve to — and they are not the same thing as closure scope, which interviews love to test.

blocks.text: When JavaScript runs, the engine creates execution contexts. The global execution context exists for the lifetime of the script. Each function invocation creates a new function execution context with its own variable environment (bindings for `var`, `let`, `const`, parameters) and a reference to the outer lexical environment (scope chain). The call stack is the data structure holding which function is currently running — last in, first out. Hoisting is the compile-phase behavior where `var` and function declarations are registered before line-by-line execution; `let` and `const` are hoisted but sit in the temporal dead zone until their declaration line. In C#, locals exist in a stack frame with definite assignment rules — no `var` hoisting surprise and no temporal dead zone.

entries.plainDefinition: An internal record of where code is running: variable bindings, `this` binding, and outer scope link.
entries.example: Calling `fetchUser()` creates a new execution context linked to the global one.

entries.plainDefinition: A stack of active function execution contexts. When a function returns, its frame pops off.
entries.example: `main → parse → validate` means three frames; `validate` is on top.

entries.plainDefinition: The period from entering a scope until a `let` or `const` declaration runs. Accessing the name throws ReferenceError.
entries.example: `console.log(x); let x = 1;` throws before line two executes.

blocks.text: Stack overflow happens when recursion or mutual calls exceed the engine's stack limit — a synchronous error, not an async one. Hoisting explains why `var` is `undefined` before its line but `let` throws. The scope chain (lexical nesting) is separate from the call stack (who called whom): a closure captures lexical outer variables even after the outer function returned and its stack frame popped. Interviews conflate "execution context" with "closure scope" — you need both models. C# closures also capture outer locals, but without `var` hoisting or TDZ; `async`/`await` in C# suspends without blocking the thread, while JavaScript `await` yields to the event loop.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: Call stack = who is running now (LIFO). Scope chain = where names are looked up (lexical nesting). Closures keep the outer lexical environment alive after the outer function returns.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Caller invokes function
items.body: Engine creates a new execution context and pushes it onto the call stack.

items.title: Creation phase
items.body: Parameters bound, `var` hoisted as `undefined`, function declarations fully hoisted, `let`/`const` registered in TDZ.

items.title: Execution phase
items.body: Lines run top to bottom. Assignments update bindings. Returns pop the frame.

items.title: Scope lookup
items.body: Unresolved names walk the scope chain outward — not up the call stack unless lexical nesting matches.

snippet.label: Hoisting: var vs let
snippet.explanation: `var` declarations hoist with initializer `undefined`. `let`/`const` hoist but cannot be read until the declaration line. Function declarations hoist the whole function.

snippet.label: Call stack trace
snippet.explanation: The stack trace lists call stack frames from innermost to outermost. This is synchronous — async stacks need `async` stack traces or source maps.

snippet.label: Closure vs call stack
snippet.explanation: The closure holds the outer lexical environment, not a stack frame. `count` lives on the heap as part of the closure — similar to C# compiler-generated closure classes capturing locals.

snippet.label: var in loops — classic pitfall
snippet.explanation: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted once. `let` in a `for` loop gets a fresh binding per iteration — the scope chain each closure captures differs.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Confusing call stack with scope chain — `inner` can read `outer`'s variable because of lexical nesting, not because `outer` is still on the stack. Using `var` in loops with async callbacks and expecting per-iteration values. Assuming hoisting means assignment runs early — only declarations hoist, not initializers. Saying closures "keep the stack frame" — they keep the lexical environment; the frame may be gone.

interviewTakeaways: Execution context = variable environment + scope chain + `this`. Call stack tracks active contexts LIFO.
Hoisting: `var` → `undefined`; `let`/`const` → TDZ until declaration; function declarations hoist fully.
Closures capture lexical outer bindings on the heap — survives after outer function returns.
60s: Stack is who runs now. Scope chain is lexical lookup. Closures keep outer env, not stack frames. var hoists; let has TDZ. Loop var vs let changes closure behavior.
Follow-up: why does `for (var i...)` with setTimeout print 3 three times?
commonPitfalls: Equating execution context with closure — context is the mechanism; closure is a function plus captured lexical environment.
Using `var` in async loops and blaming the event loop instead of hoisting.
Strong answer: 'Stack LIFO for calls. Scope chain lexical. Closure = function + outer env on heap. let per-iteration in for loops.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# closures capture locals into compiler-generated display classes. JavaScript closures capture lexical environments — same idea, different implementation, plus JS hoisting quirks C# lacks.
TypeScript emits `let`/`const` as-is. No compile-time change to hoisting or TDZ — behavior is identical to JavaScript at run time.
